comments.author: godexsoft
comments.body:
We recently merged a refactor to `develop` that enables clang-tidy's `readability-identifier-naming`. Your branch now has heavy conflicts that are largely mechanical. Below is a workflow that aligns your branch's naming with develop _before_ merging, which should minimize the merge conflicts.

## One-time setup

If you don't already have clang-tidy working in your env, on macOS:

```bash
brew install llvm@21
# Follow brew's hint to put $(brew --prefix llvm@21)/bin on PATH so run-clang-tidy is found.
```

## Workflow on your branch (before merging develop)

**1. Grab the new `.clang-tidy` from develop without pulling anything else.** Sync your fork on GitHub first, then:

```bash
git remote -v   # should show 'upstream' among others; if not:
# git remote set-url upstream git@github.com:XRPLF/rippled.git
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/develop -- .clang-tidy
```

**2. Reconfigure conan/cmake so `compile_commands.json` is fresh.**

**3. Apply renames for the files modified in your PR:**

```bash
git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD upstream/develop) HEAD \
  | grep -E '\.(cpp|h|hpp|ipp)$' \
  | xargs run-clang-tidy -p build -fix -allow-no-checks
# or -p .build, or whatever your build dir is called
```

**4. Build + test, then commit as a single dedicated commit:**

```bash
cmake --build build -j8
git commit -am "refactor: Align identifier naming with develop"
```

**5. Now merge develop:**

```bash
git merge upstream/develop
```

## Extra

Run clang-tidy once more after the merge to catch any stragglers introduced from develop's side:

```bash
run-clang-tidy -p build -fix -allow-no-checks src tests
# or -p .build, or whatever your build dir is called
```

reviewCommentsList.author: sublimator
mvadari
reviewCommentsList.body:
This PR is still a draft because I'm not 100% on the design. Happy to discuss strategies on the fix front.
My concern with adding a nested multisign feature is around performance/DoS risk. If we want to solve this problem ASAP, I would prefer a fix strategy first - I don't think that has to be mutually exclusive with adding a feature amendment in the future.

reviewCommentsList.author: sublimator
reviewCommentsList.body:
Thanks for the response

> I would prefer a fix strategy first 

Ok, that makes sense :) 

> I'm not 100% on the design. 

On further consideration I'm starting to have some hesitations too despite the elegance.  

I just spent a bit of time looking into the motivating case for some of the nested multisign work and what strikes me is that at every txn what each party did was perfectly valid and could not have been caught at signer list/{master,regular}key modification time. 

The state occurred as a coordination problem between parties. So in that case at least, automatically enabling the master key on the primary account would be based on a signing party's independent action, which would not be considered a standard practice. 

> My concern with adding a nested multisign feature is around performance/DoS risk.

Yeah, that's definitely something something that needs tightening.

What would you consider reasonable bounds on:
- Max signing depth
- Total signatures 
- Max entries per signer array
- Any other you can think of 

We're currently using depth <= 4, <= 32 entries per array, and up to 64 total signatures (the latter might be overly generous in the context of your concerns? ) 

?

Thanks

reviewCommentsList.author: mvadari
reviewCommentsList.body:
> So in that case at least, automatically enabling the master key on the primary account would be based on a signing party's independent action, which would not be considered a standard practice.

The master key would not be enabled on the primary account, it would only be usable as a signer in a signer list.

Discussion on a feature version should not be a part of this PR. That should be discussed in the XLS repo, so that it's not impossible to find later.

reviewCommentsList.author: sublimator
reviewCommentsList.body:
Wherever you are still happy to discuss then, can you link somewhere? 

I might have misunderstood or miscommunicated my understanding of the master key allowance here. I will check when on laptop again 

Thanks :)

reviewCommentsList.author: mvadari
reviewCommentsList.body: There is a discussion open in the XRPL-Standards repo on this topic.

reviewCommentsList.author: sublimator
reviewCommentsList.body:
2026 problems. I was looking at this with an agent while working with an agent on something completely unrelated. My apologies. 

> The master key would not be enabled on the primary account, it would only be usable as a signer in a signer list.

Ok, so the idea is that someone who has sole access to their master key will be able to use it for multisign purposes regardless of their master key enabled status? Though there's no real protocol method of enforcing sole access, unfortunately :/ 

I will have to double check as I'm paranoid now, so I'll get back to you with on it, but from what I saw today it's possible (and has been seen on mainnet) to create a signer list of mutable accounts, and then those accounts to change their own signing configuration such that the signer list set that was perfectly valid becomes invalid.

For example, if a subsigner disabled their master key and set up their own signer list, unless you changed the owner indexing of SignerList (sic? the lt) you'd not be able to determine what signer lists they are part of in order to disable the operations. 

> There is a discussion open in the XRPL-Standards repo on this topic.

Noted

reviewCommentsList.author: mvadari
reviewCommentsList.body:
> I will have to double check as I'm paranoid now, so I'll get back to you with on it, but from what I saw today it's possible (and has been seen on mainnet) to create a signer list of mutable accounts, and then those accounts to change their own signing configuration such that the signer list set that was perfectly valid becomes invalid.

Yes, agreed. That's why it's not enough to just try to prevent the situation - we can't 100% prevent the situation. We have to also make it easier for people to fix their configuration.

We could theoretically limit the otherwise-disabled master key to only be used on SignerListSet transactions, but that's basically equivalent to allowing all transactions, given that SignerListSet is an auth modification tx.

reviewCommentsList.author: sublimator
reviewCommentsList.body: Yeah, I can't really see any way of eking out special allowances that doesn't break existing semantics and guarantees. It might be in the end that the feature is the fix?

reviewCommentsList.author: mvadari
reviewCommentsList.body: The feature isn't without its own issues, as mentioned above. Any software decision is always about tradeoffs.

prs.body:
## High Level Overview of Change

This PR allows users to submit `simulate` requests from a multisign account without needing to specify the accounts that are doing the multisigning, and fixes an error with `simulate` that allowed double-"signed" (both single-sign and multi-sign public keys are provided) transactions.

### Context of Change

There was some confusion about how to use `simulate` with a multisign account. Receiving `tefMASTER_DISABLED` was unexpected. This change makes it more intuitive.

### Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

### API Impact

- [x] Public API: Non-breaking change

## Before / After

**Before:** 
Submitting a `simulate` request for a transaction from an account with the master key disabled and a multisig setup would result in `tefMASTER_DISABLED`. 
You can submit a `simulate` request with both `SigningPubKey` and `Signers`.

**After:**
Submitting a `simulate` request for a transaction from an account with the master key disabled and a multisig setup ignores signature checking completely (unless `Signers` is provided in any way, shape, or form).
Submitting a `simulate` request with both `SigningPubKey` and `Signers` results in `temINVALID`.

## Test Plan

Tests were adjusted and CI passes.

reviewCommentsList.author: vinniefalco
reviewCommentsList.body: Lambdas are harder to format. Especially when you specify multiple captured variables and also an argument list. In the vast majority of cases, we use lambdas as a notational convenience for things like performing initialization. In theory one can write a lambda that captures a reference to a local variable, where the lambda outlives the scope in which it is created. But we don't write code like this much at all, and when we do, we capture variables individually. I prefer an unobtrusive default capture over naming each captured variable, for the case where the lambda's lifetime is short (i.e. in the scope of the function containing the variables it captures).

prs.author: scottschurr

comments.author: scottschurr
comments.body: Squashed, rebased, and incorporated a couple of comments from @nbougalis.

prs.body:
With this changeset two-level multisigning is removed from the
codebase and replaced with single-level multisigning.  There are
three known missing elements:
1. Multisigned transactions should require higher fees than
   regular (single-signed) transaction.  That's not yet
   implemented.
2. It should be possible to disable the master key on an account
   if that account is multisign enabled (has a signer list).
   That's not yet implemented.
3. Documentation about multisigning needs to be improved.

Multisigning is still compiled out of the code base.  To enable
multisigning for a stand-alone rippled, change the
RIPPLE_ENABLE_MULTI_SIGN macro (in BeastConfig.h) to "1" and
rebuild.

This commit also addresses:
 o RIPD-912: Remove multisign APIs from STObject, and
 o RIPD-944: Replace common_transactor with jtx at call sites.

Reviewers: @nbougalis, @JoelKatz, @vinniefalco
prs.head: scottschurr:simple-m-of-n

comments.body: Incorporated as ef511282709a6a0721b504c6b7703f9de3eecf38.

prs.body:
This pull request consist of three commits:
- The first commit is a duplicate of a commit that has already passed review.  Later commits in this branch have a dependency on this first commit.  However, since that commit has already passed review, reviewers do not need to review it.
- The middle commit is tiny and provides a facility that the last commit relies on.  It allows software outside of the transactors (e.g., RPC handlers) to access the Rules.  I left this as a separate commit since it is independent of the other two.  However the last two commits could be squashed together.
- The final commit does the actual work of switching multisign from being compile-time enabled to being run-time enabled with a Feature.  This commit removes the RIPPLE_ENABLE_MULTI_SIGN macro and replaces it with a "featureMultiSign" check.  The Feature checks are modeled after those used to enable SusPay.

You can now enable multisign on a local standalone rippled by adding a Feature to the config file.  To do so, add a section like this:

```
[features]
MultiSign
```

There is a minor issue.  The `sign_for` and `submit_multisigned` RPC commands are only enabled if multisign is enabled.  However those commands are still shown in the help message even if multisign is disabled.  This is because the code that produces the help message doesn't read the config file (where the Features are kept).  This problem will become irrelevant once multisign is enabled onto the network.

Reviewers: @nbougalis @vinniefalco
prs.head: scottschurr:simple-m-of-n-feature
